title: MATH GAOKAO - 314
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Binomial Probability for Exactly Two Successes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly two successes in a fixed number of independent trials.
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed \(3\) times. Find the probability of getting exactly \(2\) heads.
questions.explanation:
The number of heads follows a binomial distribution with \(n=3\), \(p=\frac12\), and \(k=2\). Thus,
\[
P(X=2)=\binom{3}{2}\left(\frac12\right)^2\left(\frac12\right)^1
=3\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12
=\frac{3}{8}.
\]
questions.hint: Use the binomial coefficient to count the arrangements of two heads among three tosses.

questions.concept: Binomial Probability for Exactly One Success
questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly one success in repeated independent trials.
questions.question: A fair die is rolled \(4\) times. Find the probability of getting a \(6\) exactly once.
questions.explanation:
The probability of getting a \(6\) is \(\frac16\), and the probability of not getting a \(6\) is \(\frac56\). Using the binomial formula with \(n=4\), \(k=1\),
\[
P(X=1)=\binom{4}{1}\left(\frac16\right)^1\left(\frac56\right)^3
=4\cdot\frac16\cdot\frac{125}{216}
=\frac{500}{1296}
=\frac{125}{324}.
\]
questions.hint: Use the binomial formula with \(p=\frac16\) and \(q=\frac56\).

questions.concept: Probability of At Least One Success
questions.learningObjective: Use the complement rule to find the probability of at least one success in repeated independent trials.
questions.question: A biased coin has probability \(\frac14\) of landing heads. It is tossed \(3\) times. Find the probability of getting at least one head.
questions.explanation:
The complement of “at least one head” is “no heads.” Since the probability of tails is \(\frac34\),
\[
P(\text{no heads})=\left(\frac34\right)^3=\frac{27}{64}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
P(\text{at least one head})=1-\frac{27}{64}=\frac{37}{64}.
\]
questions.hint: Consider the complement event “no heads” and use independence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability that an event never occurs in repeated independent trials.
questions.question: An experiment succeeds with probability \(0.2\). It is repeated \(5\) times independently. Find the probability of no successes.
questions.explanation:
The probability of failure in one trial is \(1-0.2=0.8\). For no successes in \(5\) independent trials,
\[
P(\text{no successes})=(0.8)^5=0.32768.
\]
questions.hint: Multiply the probability of failure in each trial.

questions.concept: Binomial Probability for Exactly Two Successes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly two successes in four independent trials.
questions.question: An event occurs with probability \(\frac13\) in each of \(4\) independent trials. Find the probability that it occurs exactly twice.
questions.explanation:
Using the binomial formula with \(n=4\), \(k=2\), \(p=\frac13\), and \(q=\frac23\),
\[
P(X=2)=\binom{4}{2}\left(\frac13\right)^2\left(\frac23\right)^2
=6\cdot\frac19\cdot\frac49
=\frac{24}{81}
=\frac{8}{27}.
\]

questions.concept: Probability of At Least Two Successes
questions.learningObjective: Use complements to compute the probability of at least two successes in four independent trials.
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed \(4\) times. Find the probability of getting at least \(2\) heads.
questions.explanation:
The complement of “at least two heads” is “0 or 1 head.” Since there are \(2^4=16\) equally likely outcomes,
\[
P(0\text{ heads})=\frac{1}{16},\qquad
P(1\text{ head})=\frac{4}{16}.
\]
Thus,
\[
P(\text{at least 2 heads})=1-\frac{1}{16}-\frac{4}{16}=\frac{11}{16}.
\]
questions.hint: Use the complement and count the cases with 0 or 1 head.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability that every trial results in success.
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed \(5\) times. Find the probability that all tosses are heads.
questions.explanation:
Each toss is independent with probability \(\frac12\) of heads. Therefore,
\[
P(\text{all heads})=\left(\frac12\right)^5=\frac{1}{32}.
\]
questions.hint: All five tosses must be heads; multiply the probabilities.

questions.concept: Binomial Probability for Exactly Three Successes
questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly three successes in five independent trials.
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed \(5\) times. Find the probability of getting exactly \(3\) heads.
questions.hint: Use the binomial coefficient to count arrangements of exactly three heads.

questions.concept: Probability of At Most One Success
questions.learningObjective: Compute the probability of at most one success in three independent trials.
questions.question: An event occurs with probability \(0.1\) in each of \(3\) independent trials. Find the probability that it occurs at most once.
questions.hint: At most one success means 0 or 1 success; add those two probabilities.

questions.concept: Probability of At Least Four Successes
questions.learningObjective: Apply the binomial formula to compute a cumulative probability for repeated independent trials.
questions.question: A basketball player makes each free throw independently with probability \(0.8\). She takes \(5\) free throws. Find the probability that she makes at least \(4\) of them.
questions.explanation:
At least \(4\) made means exactly \(4\) or exactly \(5\) made. Using the binomial formula,
\[
P(X=4)=\binom{5}{4}(0.8)^4(0.2)=5(0.4096)(0.2)=0.4096,
\]
and
\[
P(X=5)=(0.8)^5=0.32768.
\]
Therefore,
\[
P(X\ge 4)=0.4096+0.32768=0.73728.
\]
questions.hint: At least four made means exactly 4 or exactly 5 made; use the binomial formula for each and add.
